content: Liver cancer, also known as hepatic cancer, includes malignant tumors such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma originating in the liver. It develops when liver cells undergo abnormal growth due to genetic mutations triggered by chronic liver damage, infections, toxins, or metabolic conditions. Common causes include chronic hepatitis B or C virus infections, alcohol-related liver disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and exposure to aflatoxins. Liver cancer often arises in the context of cirrhosis, a scarring process reducing liver function. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice, and fatigue, but early stages can be silent, complicating diagnosis. Diagnostic evaluation involves blood tests measuring alpha-fetoprotein, imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT, or MRI, and biopsy in some cases. Treatment depends on stage and liver function and may include surgical resection, liver transplantation, ablative therapies, chemotherapy, targeted agents, or immunotherapy. Lifestyle modifications like reducing alcohol intake, vaccination against hepatitis B, and managing metabolic risk factors support prevention and long-term care. Understanding liver cancer's diverse presentations and approaches is critical for patient education and safety. This module presents clear definitions, mechanisms, clinical details, and evidence-based guidance. Limitations include variable prognosis based on tumor stage and liver function, and safety considerations encompass treatment side effects and liver toxicity risk. Synonyms include hepatic cancer, hepatic carcinoma, and specific subtypes such as hepatoma. This comprehensive resource is designed for retrieval-oriented learning and patient-centered communication.

content: Liver cancer refers to malignant tumors that originate in the liver. The most common type is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), arising from hepatocytes, or liver cells. Another type is cholangiocarcinoma, originating from bile duct cells inside the liver. These tumors can impair liver function and spread to other organs. Liver cancer differs from metastatic liver tumors, where cancer spreads to the liver from other body parts. Understanding the types helps guide diagnosis and treatment.

chunk_title: Causes and Risk Factors of Liver Cancer
content: Several causes and risk factors contribute to liver cancer development. The primary cause worldwide is chronic infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV), which cause ongoing liver inflammation and damage. Other contributors include alcohol-related liver disease, leading to cirrhosis, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), often linked to obesity and diabetes. Exposure to aflatoxins, toxins produced by certain molds in contaminated food, can also increase risk. Genetic conditions and certain inherited diseases may contribute but are less common. These risk factors induce chronic liver injury, scarring, and genetic mutations, increasing cancer likelihood.

chunk_title: Symptoms and Clinical Presentation of Liver Cancer
content: Liver cancer symptoms often develop late and may be vague. Common symptoms include abdominal pain or fullness, especially under the right ribs, unintended weight loss, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, and jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes. Enlarged liver or spleen and swelling of the abdomen due to fluid accumulation (ascites) can arise. Early-stage liver cancer often causes no symptoms, making surveillance important in at-risk populations. Recognizing symptoms helps prompt timely evaluation.

chunk_title: Diagnosis and Evaluation of Liver Cancer
content: Evaluating suspected liver cancer involves several tests. Blood tests include liver function tests and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), a tumor marker elevated in many cases of HCC. Imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide detailed views of liver lesions. Biopsy, the removal of a small tissue sample, may be needed to confirm diagnosis in unclear cases. Non-invasive imaging criteria often suffice for diagnosis in patients with known cirrhosis. Accurate diagnosis guides treatment planning and prognosis assessment.

chunk_title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Liver Cancer
content: Liver cancer arises from complex cellular and molecular changes initiated by chronic liver injury. Repeated damage from viruses, toxins, or metabolic disorders causes inflammation, scarring (fibrosis), and eventually cirrhosis. This environment fosters genetic mutations that disrupt cell cycle regulation, enabling uncontrolled cell growth. Signal transduction pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin and p53 tumor suppressor pathways, are often altered. Angiogenesis or new blood vessel formation also supports tumor growth. Understanding these mechanisms informs development of targeted therapies.

chunk_title: Types and Subtypes of Liver Cancer
content: The majority of liver cancers are hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for over 75% of cases. Cholangiocarcinoma, a cancer of bile duct epithelial cells, is less common but has distinct behavior and treatment. Secondary (metastatic) liver tumors originate from cancers elsewhere, such as colon or breast cancer, but are not primary liver cancer. Other rare primary liver tumors include angiosarcoma and hepatoblastoma, typically in children. Knowing tumor types aids in prognosis and management planning.

chunk_title: Treatment and Management of Liver Cancer
content: Treatment depends on tumor size, number, spread, and liver function. Potential curative options include surgical resection or liver transplantation for eligible patients. Locoregional therapies such as radiofrequency ablation, transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), or selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) target tumors in the liver without surgery. Systemic therapies include targeted drugs (e.g., sorafenib) and immunotherapy to inhibit tumor growth. Palliative care also plays an important role in symptom management and quality of life. Multidisciplinary care involving surgeons, oncologists, and hepatologists optimizes outcomes.

content: Preventing liver cancer includes addressing modifiable risk factors. Vaccination against hepatitis B reduces infection risk. Treatment for hepatitis C can decrease liver damage. Limiting alcohol use prevents chronic liver disease. Maintaining a healthy weight and managing diabetes reduce risk from fatty liver disease. Avoidance of aflatoxin-contaminated foods is also recommended. Lifestyle measures support general liver health and cancer prevention.

chunk_title: Safety and Side Effects during Liver Cancer Treatment
content: Treatments for liver cancer can have significant side effects. Surgery and transplantation pose risks of bleeding, infection, and liver failure in some cases. Locoregional therapies may cause pain, fever, or liver inflammation. Systemic therapies can lead to fatigue, skin reactions, hypertension, or blood abnormalities. Careful monitoring and supportive care minimize harm. Patients should disclose all medications and follow safety instructions provided by their healthcare team.

content: A common misconception is that liver cancer only affects people who drink alcohol heavily; however, viral hepatitis and metabolic diseases also cause liver cancer. Another false belief is that liver cancer always causes early symptoms; in reality, it can be silent until advanced. Some think liver cancer is incurable; while prognosis can be poor, early detection and treatment can improve chances of survival. Correcting these misunderstandings promotes awareness and timely care.

chunk_title: Prognosis and Outcomes in Liver Cancer
content: Prognosis depends on tumor stage, size, number, spread, and underlying liver function. Early-stage tumors amenable to surgery or transplantation have better survival rates. Advanced disease or poor liver function worsens outcomes. Regular surveillance in at-risk groups helps detect liver cancer earlier. Ongoing research is improving treatment and survival. Understanding prognosis helps patients and clinicians make informed decisions about care.
